title: Backend can link repeated GPS updates to the same child over time
description: The flow carries live GPS coordinates at regular intervals from the child's device to the backend. Even if each individual update seems innocuous, the backend can associate successive updates with the same child/account/device and build a persistent movement history, enabling strong linkability across sessions and observations.

title: Live GPS stream enables identification of the child

assumptions: Assumes GPS coordinates are sufficiently precise and that the backend operator or a party with access to backend data can correlate locations with known places or auxiliary data.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate; the threat itself is strong even if the exact sub-node reference differs in a given tree version.

title: Continuous location updates expose the child's presence and activities

uncertainty_note: Selected as a best-fit detectability threat focused on observation of the child's activities via this live-location flow.

title: Continuous location sharing enables detailed disclosure of habits and sensitive inferences
description: A live location stream can reveal home, school, worship, healthcare visits, social relationships, and daily routines. Sharing this data with a secondary guardian may disclose more detail than needed for the purpose of limited child monitoring.
assumptions: Location updates are sufficiently frequent and precise to permit inference of sensitive places and habits.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is a best-fit for excessive information disclosure from a detailed location stream.

title: Secondary guardian may be unaware of data accuracy, retention, or further-use implications
description: The backend's grant-and-share flow may not adequately inform the recipient about how live location is sourced, how current or accurate it is, how long access lasts, whether data is retained, or whether onward sharing is permitted. This creates privacy risks through misunderstanding and misuse.
assumptions: The system may not present clear notices, labels, or contextual explanations during access grant and live sharing.
uncertainty_note: Best-fit unawareness threat; applicability depends on the transparency UX around granting and sharing.

title: Sharing live location with a secondary guardian may exceed consent or purpose limitations
description: Granting a secondary guardian access to the child's live location may be incompatible with the original consent, legal basis, custody arrangement, or purpose limitation under which the location was collected. If the grant is broader than authorized, the flow creates a policy and compliance violation.
assumptions: Access rights may depend on parental consent, court orders, age of the child, jurisdiction, or explicit purpose restrictions.
uncertainty_note: Best-fit non-compliance threat; exact legal/policy basis is context-dependent.

title: Partner-shared analytics may be linkable to other datasets or partner-held identifiers
description: Even if the backend shares 'aggregated' usage and engagement analytics, the partner may be able to link repeated reports, segment-level metrics, timestamps, campaign metadata, app/version identifiers, or regional breakdowns with its existing datasets to infer behavior about the same user groups or, in edge cases, particular users. The sharing action itself enables cross-context linkability beyond the app's original context.
assumptions: Assumes the shared analytics include stable dimensions, time windows, cohort attributes, campaign/ad identifiers, device/platform splits, or other metadata that can be correlated by the partner across reports or with external data.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node assignment is based on best judgement because the retrieved context only confirmed threat-type applicability for Process->ExternalEntity, not detailed subtree ids.

title: Aggregated analytics may still permit identification of individuals or small cohorts
description: If the backend shares coarse-looking analytics but some aggregates are over small populations, rare usage patterns, narrow time windows, or granular demographic/region segments, the partner may infer the identity of individuals or uniquely identifiable groups. Repeated disclosures can further sharpen identification.
assumptions: Assumes aggregation thresholds, k-anonymity-style minimum cohort sizes, or suppression rules may be absent or inconsistently enforced.
uncertainty_note: Applies only if the aggregation is insufficiently privacy-preserving; if robust aggregation and suppression are enforced, this threat may be reduced.

title: Partner can derive sensitive insights from received engagement analytics
description: The advertising/analytics partner may derive sensitive information from usage and engagement patterns, such as probable interests, lifestyle, health-related app usage, religion, political affinity, or vulnerable status, especially when analytics are segmented by feature usage, geography, time, or campaign. Such derivation may occur even if explicit sensitive fields are not shared.
assumptions: Assumes the app's usage patterns can correlate with sensitive categories or that the partner combines the received analytics with its broader profiling datasets.
uncertainty_note: Sensitivity depends on the app domain and metric granularity; if the app is not sensitive and only high-level totals are shared, impact may be lower.

title: Users may be unaware that backend analytics are shared with a third-party partner for monetization
description: Sharing analytics with an advertising/analytics partner to fund the free tier may not be sufficiently visible or understandable to users. If users do not realize that their app usage contributes to partner-facing analytics disclosures, they cannot form an accurate mental model of downstream processing.
assumptions: Assumes notices are buried, vague, or do not clearly explain third-party analytics sharing and monetization purposes.
uncertainty_note: This is inferred from the described business model; actual applicability depends on the clarity and timing of user-facing notices.

title: Sharing analytics for advertising/monetization may exceed or conflict with user consent and purpose limitation
description: If users provided data for service operation or basic analytics but not for disclosure to an advertising/analytics partner to fund the free tier, the backend's sharing may violate consent expectations, purpose limitation, or other privacy obligations. Aggregation does not automatically remove compliance duties if the data remains personal or household-related in context.
assumptions: Assumes consent, legitimate-interest balancing, opt-out rights, contractual restrictions, or regional legal requirements may not explicitly cover this partner sharing for monetization.
uncertainty_note: Legal/compliance applicability is jurisdiction- and implementation-specific; tree-node assignment is based on best judgement rather than a retrieved subtree mapping.

title: Check-in/SOS messages can be linked to the same child over time
description: The backend receives repeated manual check-in / SOS messages containing the child's location. If messages carry a stable child/account/device identifier, or are otherwise linkable via metadata, the backend can correlate multiple events and build a history of the child's movements and emergency behavior.
assumptions: Assumes the flow contains a persistent identifier, account binding, device token, or similar metadata enabling correlation across messages.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context did not include specific linkability subtree entries.

title: Location-bearing SOS/check-in message identifies the child
description: A manual check-in / SOS message with current location is inherently identifying or highly identifying when tied to a child account, device, or parent-child relationship. The backend can associate the message with a specific child and infer presence at a particular place and time.
assumptions: Assumes the backend can associate the message with a specific child user, directly or indirectly.
uncertainty_note: Specific identifiability subtree id not present in retrieved context; node chosen by best judgement.

title: Attributed SOS/check-in records may prevent plausible denial by the child
description: The backend may store a record showing that a specific child sent a check-in or SOS from a certain location and time. Such attributable evidence can later be used to claim the child initiated the message, reducing their ability to repudiate the action.
assumptions: Assumes messages are logged with sender identity/account, timestamps, and possibly authentication data.

title: The flow discloses precise location and distress context to the backend
description: This data flow reveals the child's current location together with the fact that they initiated a manual check-in or SOS. That discloses sensitive contextual information about whereabouts, routines, and potentially an emergency situation to the receiving backend.
assumptions: Assumes the location is reasonably precise and the backend has access to the message contents in identifiable form.
uncertainty_note: Specific disclosure subtree id selected by best judgement because the retrieved context did not include disclosure nodes.

title: The backend can derive behavior patterns and risk inferences from repeated location check-ins/SOS events
description: Even if only current location is sent per message, the backend can aggregate messages over time to infer routines, frequent places, school/home locations, movement patterns, supervision gaps, and possible distress episodes. These derived insights go beyond the explicitly provided data.
assumptions: Assumes the service stores or can analyze multiple historical messages from the same child.
uncertainty_note: Specific detectability/disclosure distinction can be model-dependent; here this is treated as detectability/derivation in line with LINDDUN's inference concern, but exact subtree id is approximate.

title: Child may be unaware of backend-side use and retention of SOS/location data
description: A child sending a check-in or SOS may not understand that the backend can store, analyze, and further process the location and emergency-context data, including retention duration, operational monitoring, and possible secondary uses. This creates a risk that processing is insufficiently transparent to the child.
assumptions: Assumes notices are not fully understandable, visible, or age-appropriate for the child user.
uncertainty_note: Unawareness applies if transparency to the child is weak; if strong age-appropriate notice is present, this threat may be reduced.

title: Processing of child location and SOS data may exceed necessity or valid consent/authority
description: The backend processes highly sensitive child location and emergency-related data. If collection, storage, or onward use is broader than necessary for delivering the check-in/SOS function, or lacks an appropriate legal basis / parental authorization / child-appropriate consent handling, the flow creates non-compliance risk.
assumptions: Assumes the system is subject to privacy/data-protection obligations regarding children's location data and emergency-context processing.
uncertainty_note: Exact non-compliance subtree depends on jurisdiction and the implemented legal basis; node id chosen by best judgement.
